earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog lists only wordlist/classification items (Tryon & Hackman 1983 Solomon Islands Languages) and ethnography (Russell 1951); no grammar or phonology of Fataleka exists

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page for Fataleka (fata1245).
sources.note: Bibliographic only; three references (Tryon & Hackman 1983, Siegel 1986, Russell 1950), none a grammar, sketch or phonology; Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology.

sources.citation: OLAC: Resources in and about the Fataleka language [far] (Internet Archive copy of Dec 2024).
sources.note: Catalog only. Lists no language description for Fataleka: Capell PARADISEC recordings (AC1-415, AC1-433) and a Swadesh list (AC2-SINMALA102), Simons 1980 (Malaitan pronoun systems), a 1980 West Fataleka book of Jonah, Ethnologue and Glottolog entries.

sources.citation: Hashizume, Daisaku (橋爪太作). 2020. 土地と向き合う人々: ソロモン諸島マライタ島北部における森林伐採の展開と土地-自己知識の真理性について [The People Who Face with Their Ancestral Land]. 文化人類学 (Japanese Journal of Cultural Anthropology) 85(2): 206-. DOI 10.14890/jjcanth.85.2_206. (Related: JRCA 21(2): 59-, 2020, English version DOI 10.14890/jrca.21.2_59; 文化人類学 87(1), 2022, DOI 10.14890/jjcanth.87.1_005; book 大地を切り裂く人々, 2025.)
sources.note: No phonology content and no note on transcription (searched 表記, アクセント, 声調, 強勢, 発音, 声門, 正書法). Useful negative evidence: footnote 3 reviews all prior research on the Fataleka area and names only Russell 1950 (colonial report), Guidieri 1980 (symbolic anthropology of mortuary ritual), Moore 1981 (Bina clan genealogies, East Fataleka) and Miyauchi 2011 (sociology, Anokelo village) - no linguistic description is known to the most recent long-term fieldworker.
sources.venue: 文化人類学 (Japanese Journal of Cultural Anthropology)

sources.citation: Farongoe Lea Ana Fataleka: Fataleka New Testament. SITAG / Wycliffe Bible Translators, 2017 (eBible.org id far / FARWBT).
sources.note: Scripture text in a practical orthography (details page read online); no linguistic front matter; confirms SITAG translation work exists but no accompanying phonology statement was found.

sources.citation: Moore, Clive. 2017. Making Mala: Malaita in Solomon Islands, 1870s-1930s. Canberra: ANU Press (open access). Front matter, 'A Note on Spelling Malaitan Words', pp. xxv-xxvii (pronunciation guide 'slightly modified from Akin 2013a, xvii').
sources.note: Segmental spelling conventions for Malaitan words (b = [mb], d = [nd], g = [ng], glottal stop is a consonant never adjacent to another consonant, kw/gw/mw/ng are single consonants) plus one prosodic remark: 'Doubled vowels are pronounced as lengthened and accented (e.g., Maasina Rule).' This is a lay, pan-Malaitan (Kwaio-derived) remark about long vowels, not a statement of where Fataleka word stress falls; recorded here only as context.

sources.citation: SITAG / Wycliffe Bible Translators. 2017. Farongoe Lea Ana Fataleka (Fataleka New Testament): 'Fatae Sulia Na Farongoe Lea' (translators' introduction, INT) and 'Diksonari' (glossary, GLO). eBible.org id far / FARWBT, HTML edition generated from source files dated 12 Dec 2025.
sources.note: Nothing. The introduction (in Fataleka) covers the Hebrew/Greek originals and the translators' principles; there is no alphabet table, spelling key or pronunciation note, and the glossary is of biblical terms. The practical orthography visible in the text marks glottal stop with an apostrophe and writes long vowels double, with no accent marks.

sources.citation: Lewis, M. Paul, Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2013. Fataleka [far]. In Ethnologue: Languages of the World, 17th edition. Dallas: SIL International. (Internet Archive copy of 2013-04-23.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Nothing. The Typology field reads only 'SVO'; no stress or tone line. Dialects: 'Dialect of To'abaita [mlu] (Wurm and Hattori 1981). Intelligibility of Baeggu variety of To'abaita reportedly high, but of To'abaita much less. Lexical similarity: 82% with Kwara'ae [kwf], 76% with Lau [llu].' Language Development: literacy rates only -- no dictionary, grammar, or vernacular literature listed, consistent with the absence of any SIL/SITAG description in OLAC.

sources.citation: Wurm, S. A., P. Mühlhäusler & D. T. Tryon (eds.). 1996. Atlas of Languages of Intercultural Communication in the Pacific, Asia, and the Americas (Trends in Linguistics. Documentation 13). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter. DOI 10.1515/9783110819724. [held page-text, 1903 PDF pages]
sources.note: Data only (pronoun forms in the North Malaitan/Wai comparison table); no stress or tone statement; p. 844 merely lists 'Fataleka Liturgy & Ritual 1923'.

sources.citation: Siegel, Jeff. 1986. Wai: a Malaitan language in Fiji. In P. Geraghty, L. Carrington & S.A. Wurm (eds), FOCAL II: Papers from the Fourth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, 435-463. Pacific Linguistics C-94. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 'Wai phonology' (pp.447-448, Table 3-1) gives only the segment inventory and phonemic vowel length; no statement on stress or accent anywhere in the paper. Describes Wai, a Fiji immigrant variety derived from mixed North Malaitan dialects (Lau, To'abaita, Baelelea, Baegu, Fataleka), not Fataleka as spoken on Malaita.

sources.citation: Siegel, Jeff. 1985. Plantation languages in Fiji. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xvii+368 leaves. ANU Open Research hdl 1885/133340 (open; scanned PDF 205 MB + machine text 668 KB). Sec. 0.5 'Transcription' with Table 0-4 'North Malaitan phonology and orthography'; ch. 3 (origins and linguistic backgrounds of the Pacific Islands labourers, incl. Fataleka FTK); sec. 10.3 'Wai: a Malaitan language in Fiji' with 10.3.3.2 'Wai phonology'. The thesis behind Siegel 1986 (FOCAL II), which Glottolog files under fata1245.
sources.note: Nothing on stress, accent or tone for North Malaitan, Fataleka or Wai. Table 0-4 is a consonant/vowel chart only; 10.3.3.2 reads 'The vowels of Wai are the same as those of both NM and Fijian, including phonemic vowel length. The consonants also appear to be basically those found in both..' and then treats f > v, prenasalisation of voiced stops, loss of the glottal stop ('ave (Lau 'afe) wife') and of To'abaita/Baelelea interdental fricative. a full-text search for stress/accent/penultimate/syllable over the whole text hits only Pidgin Fijian ('Some words.. have come into PPF with stress on th…

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B.D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands languages: an internal classification. Pacific Linguistics C-72. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Fataleka is wordlist no. 68; comparative wordlists and reflex/sound-correspondence tables only. a full-text search for stress/accent/penultimate finds nothing relevant; no prosodic statement for any language.

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. 1982. Word taboo and comparative Austronesian linguistics. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 3: Accent on variety, 157-226. Pacific Linguistics C-76. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Fataleka appears only in the list of Malaitan languages used for the lexicostatistical/word-taboo study; no phonology; 'stress'/'accent' absent (only 'Accent on variety' in the volume title).
sources.venue: Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1982. Towards a classification of Solomon Islands languages. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 97-108. Pacific Linguistics C-74. Canberra: ANU.

sources.citation: Huebner, Thom (comp.). 1979. Solomon Islands Pijin: Special Skills Handbook (Peace Corps Language Handbook Series). Brattleboro, VT: Experiment in International Living / SIL. ERIC ED205041. Appendix 'List of Solomon Islands vernaculars ordered according to number of speakers.. indication given of published literature' (adapted from a 1975 Ministry of Agriculture and Lands, Honiara, list).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: No phonology. The entry reads: 'Fataleka (MN) North Central Malaita. 2,600. Orthography available - Kwara'ae may serve. MM Hymn Book.' i.e. as of 1975-79 the only vernacular literature was a Melanesian Mission hymn book and no separate linguistic description existed; pointer value only (confirms absence of a grammar/dictionary, cf. entries for Sa'a, Arosi, Roviana that do cite grammars).
sources.venue: Brattleboro, VT: Experiment in International Living / SIL

sources.citation: Simons, Gary F. [1977]. Standardized alphabets for Malaitan languages. Working Papers for the Language Variation and Limits to Communication Project, No. 5. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University and Summer Institute of Linguistics. 34 pp. (fieldwork Malaita, July-Aug 1977; SIL Scholars reprint).
sources.note: Consonant alphabet and pronunciations only (b d g gw prenasalised); no stress statement for Fataleka. The paper's only stress rule (p. 19) is for Kwara'ae [kwar1239]: 'In Kwara'ae primary stress generally falls on the penultimate (second to last) syllable' (David Gegeo p.c.), given while arguing that vowel length should be written with a macron; plus a general Malaitan remark 'Length here is related to stress in that a lengthened vowel in a normally unstressed position tends to be stressed. However, length is not the same as stress.'

sources.citation: Zemp, Hugo. 1973. Fataleka and Baegu Music: Malaita, Solomon Islands. UNESCO Collection Musical Sources (Philips 6586 018). LP record; sleeve commentary by Hugo Zemp (recordings 1969-1970). Read from the scanned text of the sleeve, archive.org item lp_fataleka-and-baegu-music-malaita-solomon_fataleka-baegu.
sources.note: No phonology content. The only linguistic sentence is 'Their languages, which belong to the Melanesian group of the Austronesian family, are closely related'; the rest describes musical genres, panpipe ensembles and tunings, divinatory and funeral songs, with a few Fataleka terms (kana, uunu, 'au) given without any pronunciation or spelling note. a full-text search for stress/accent/syllab/pronunc/orthograph/spelling/glottal/vowel/tone/pitch finds only musical 'tone'/'pitches'.

sources.citation: Voegelin, C. F. & F. M. Voegelin. 1964. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Three. Anthropological Linguistics 6(9). (ERIC ED010354; Solomon Islands sections compiled from Capell 1962 and Ivens's BSOS grammars.)
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Name and population in Capell-derived subgroup listing only; the fascicle's only stress sentences are for Nakanai (New Britain) and Nggela ('Stress is non-phonemic, occurring on penultimate syllables'), per the on-disk extract's document-wide a full-text search for stress/accent.

sources.citation: Russell, T. 1950. The Fataleka of Malaita. Oceania 21(1): 1-13.
sources.note: One of only three Glottolog references; ethnographic, but could carry a brief note on the language. Very low probability of a stress statement.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. Field recordings and notes, North Malaita: PARADISEC AC1-433 'Malaita Island (north and south), Guadalcanal Island' (1970) and AC2-SINMALA102 Swadesh list.
sources.note: Only archival primary material tagged for Fataleka; Capell's notes sometimes carry accent marks or a prosodic remark. PARADISEC catalog was bot-could not be reached by automated download.

sources.citation: Ivens, Walter G. 1930. The Island Builders of the Pacific. London: Seeley, Service & Co. (archive.org item islandbuildersof0000walt, scanned text).
sources.note: pp.27-28 group the North Mala languages ('Tali Kali, Fata Leka, Kwara 'Ae are closer akin to one another..') with a few consonant remarks (prenasalisation, glottal 'break'); nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Lichtenberk, Frantisek. 2008. A Grammar of Toqabaqita. (Mouton Grammar Library 42.) Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. Ch. 2 (phonology, incl. stress).
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: a digital copy exists, HathiTrust search-only; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6254.M271 L53 2008) (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6254.M271 L53 2008
sources.note: Closest fully described North Malaitan lect (toab1237); Ross 1973 (quoted in Siegel 1986:446) holds that 'all North Malaitan dialects share essentially the same grammar'. Would supply the family-internal expectation for Fataleka stress, but only as a proxy under a different glottocode, not a Fataleka statement.
